activity: to ask for directions in a new language and understand the answer
knowledge_domain: to ask for directions in a new language and understand the answer
fact: Language learners can usually understand more words than they can say, so a learner may follow spoken directions they could not yet give themselves.
story:
The morning had started badly, and Brielle was trying to salvage it. Her dad's phone had died overnight, the printed map was back at the hotel, and somehow she had walked out of the square alone while everyone else argued over which café had the good pastries. Now she was three streets away in a town where every sign was in French, and she had exactly one sentence memorized: "Excusez-moi, où est le marché?"

She had practiced it for two days, ever since her neighbor Mr. Lombardi had given her his old phrasebook with a sticky note on the directions page. Back home, her friend Macie had quizzed her in the cafeteria, laughing when Brielle's accent turned "marché" into something like "marshmallow." "You can ask where things are," Macie had said, "but you can't understand a word of the answer." Bentley had disagreed. "You understand more than you can say," he insisted. "Everybody does. My cousin moved to Portugal and it was like that for a year." Brielle hadn't believed him. It seemed like a rule with no reason behind it, the kind of thing you couldn't check.

She stopped in front of a bakery, where a woman was sweeping crumbs off the step. Brielle's heart hammered, but she said the sentence anyway, slowly, the way she'd drilled it. "Excusez-moi, où est le marché?" The words came out whole. The woman smiled, set her broom against the doorframe, and answered in a rush of French, pointing with her free hand. "Tournez à gauche à la pharmacie, puis continuez jusqu'à l'église, et le marché est derrière l'église, à droite."

Something strange happened. Brielle caught it: gauche, left. Pharmacie, the green cross she'd passed two streets back. L'église, the church with the tall gray tower she could see over the rooftops. Derrière, behind, which she knew from the word for "back." She hadn't planned to understand any of this. She could never have said those sentences herself, not even slowly, not with the whole day to practice. Yet the woman's directions assembled themselves in her head like a picture: left at the pharmacy, straight to the church, and the market behind it. She understood every step of an answer she could never have given.

"Merci beaucoup," she managed, and the woman laughed and swept a little flour off Brielle's sleeve, as if tidying her for the journey. Brielle turned left at the green cross, kept the church tower in sight, and found her family already inside the market stalls, her dad waving between a pyramid of tomatoes. "How did you get here?" he asked. "You don't have the map." Brielle held up the phrasebook with Mr. Lombardi's sticky note fluttering on it. "The lady gave me directions," she said. "And I understood all of them. Bentley's going to lose his mind."

activity: the idea that prices rise when many people want something scarce and fall when it is plentiful
knowledge_domain: the idea that prices rise when many people want something scarce and fall when it is plentiful
fact: In 'The Wealth of Nations', published in 1776, Adam Smith pointed out that nothing is more useful than water, yet it will buy scarcely anything, while a diamond can buy a great deal.
story:
The thermometer outside Ms. Hughes's gas station read ninety-six degrees, and the parking lot shimmered like water itself. Emily and Gia leaned their bikes against the ice machine and pushed through the door into the cold breath of the air conditioning. Gia went straight for the drink cooler, which was packed so full of water bottles that they clinked when she pulled one out. Fifty cents, said the sticker, and Gia groaned happily. "At the stadium they charge four dollars for this."

Emily carried her own bottle to the counter, where Ms. Hughes was tagging a shelf of umbrellas. Last month those umbrellas had been three dollars. Tonight, with the radio promising thunderstorms by morning, the new sticker said nine. Emily turned one over in her hands and thought about the rain jacket she had almost brought that morning, and how she'd left it on the hook because the sky had been blue. That choice was the reason she was standing here now.

Behind the register, in the little glass case, sat a ring with a stone no bigger than a grain of rice. Gia spotted it and pressed her nose to the glass. "How much is that?" Ms. Hughes told her, and Gia stepped back like the number had pushed her. "That costs more than the whole cooler of water out there," she said. "Water keeps you alive and the shiny rock doesn't even do anything."

Something in Emily's memory germinated. She had read a page in Ms. Hughes's old econ book, the one she'd borrowed during the power outage last winter. She closed her eyes and pulled the sentence up. "In The Wealth of Nations, published in 1776, Adam Smith pointed out that nothing is more useful than water, yet it will buy scarcely anything, while a diamond can buy a great deal." She said it slowly, the way it had been printed, and Gia squinted at her. "Wealth of what?"

"Nations," Emily said. "It's a book." Gia looked from the ring to the cooler and back, and Emily could almost watch the question take root in her too.

Emily tested her own half-formed idea out loud. "I bet the water's fifty cents because the cooler is stuffed. And the umbrellas are nine dollars because there are only six left and everyone wants one before the storm." It came out coherent, almost a theory. She turned to Ms. Hughes. "If the cooler's still half full at closing, will the water go on sale?" Ms. Hughes rested her elbows on the counter. "Marked down every night it doesn't empty," she said. Emily bought her fifty-cent bottle and set it in her bike basket, then walked back and added an umbrella, nine dollars and almost all her savings.

Outside, the first hot wind of the storm rattled the pumps, and Gia called from her bike, "Race you home before it pours."

activity: to settle a disagreement over a game by naming the problem and agreeing on a fair rule
knowledge_domain: to settle a disagreement over a game by naming the problem and agreeing on a fair rule
fact: A fair coin toss gives each side an equal chance, which is why sports such as American football and cricket use a coin toss to decide how a game starts.
story:
Matteo had been dribbling around the cones for ten minutes when the argument started. Sandra and Brooklyn stood at half court, both gripping the same basketball, and their voices were getting louder. Sandra's team had taken the first possession at the last practice, and now Brooklyn's team wanted it, and neither of them would let go.

"We shot for it last time," Sandra said. "You lost fair and square."

"That wasn't a rule," Brooklyn said. "Nobody prescribed that. You just started shooting."

Mr. Gill blew his whistle, but instead of sorting it out himself, he tossed Matteo a coin from his pocket. "You're captain today, Matteo. Fix it."

He turned the coin over in his hand, thinking about the year before, when his old team had fallen apart over fights like this one. They had never agreed on how to decide anything, and every argument turned into a grudge. He did not want that to happen again.

"Here's the problem," he said, stepping between them. "Both teams want first possession, and we've never had a real rule for it. So we need one." He held up the coin. "A fair coin toss gives each side an equal chance. That's why sports like American football and cricket use a coin toss to decide how a game starts. It's not random someone shooting while the other team's still tying a shoe. It's actually equal."

Brooklyn squinted at him. "How do we know it's equal?"

Matteo flipped the coin ten times onto the blacktop. Six heads, four tails. Sandra crossed her arms. "That's not equal."

"Ten flips is too few to show it," Matteo said, though privately he felt a small doubt, like a crack in something that had seemed coherent a minute ago. "Try more." They flipped it thirty more times, Brooklyn calling out the results, Sandra stacking pebbles to count. Eighteen heads, twenty-two tails. Closer. Sandra studied the two little piles and slowly nodded.

"Fine," she said. "Call it in the air."

Brooklyn called heads. Matteo flipped the coin high above them all, and it spun there against the grey sky.

activity: to use loops and if-then blocks in Scratch to make a game that keeps score
knowledge_domain: to use loops and if-then blocks in Scratch to make a game that keeps score
fact: A Scratch variable keeps its value between runs, so if the score is never set to 0 at the start, a new game begins with the old total.
story:
The computer lab at Camp Windrow smelled of pine from the open windows and glue sticks from the craft table next door. Edouard had spent three mornings building his Scratch game, a maze where a cat collected stars, and each star was supposed to add one point to the score. He had loops making the stars blink and if-then blocks that said if the cat touches a star, change score by 1. It worked, mostly. He dragged the cat through the maze, watched the score climb to 57, and grinned at Nadine, who was making her own game two seats over.

"Try it," he said.

Nadine clicked the green flag and immediately frowned. "It says 57. That's not fair, I haven't even moved yet."

"That's impossible." Edouard leaned over her shoulder. The cat sat motionless at the start of the maze, and above it, in orange letters, the score read 57. He had not set it to any number at the beginning; he had only built the part that added points. He sat back and stared at his own blocks, thinking. The score could not come from nowhere, so it had to be coming from somewhere he could not see. He had a small idea about it, and he wanted to test it before he said anything out loud.

First he played the game himself until the score reached 12, then stopped everything and pressed the green flag again. The score still read 12. He pressed it three more times, and each time the old number stayed, like the game had a memory that nobody had told him about. "It keeps its value between runs," he said slowly. "The score never goes back to the start unless you make it."

"So my game starts with your leftover points?" Nadine said.

"Any leftover points. Watch." At the start of his program, right after the green flag block, he added a single block: set score to 0. He played, earned 57 points, stopped, and started again. Zero. Clean and honest.

Mr. Tse came by on his rounds and played one round, nodding at the blinking star loop. He mentioned that his colleague at the robotics table was teaching something similar next week, and that Nadine's quick hands with the mouse must be from practice, not something hereditary. After he moved on, Nadine asked Edouard to explain the fix so she could copy it.

"It's simple," he said. "I'll summarize it in one sentence. At the start of every game, set the score to zero, or the old total comes back."

She added the block to her own game, tested it twice, and the score began at 0 both times. Then she beat his high score on her first try, and the maze cat blinked its stars in the summer light.

activity: tone differences, public versus private spaces and common conventions of online communication
knowledge_domain: tone differences, public versus private spaces and common conventions of online communication
fact: Psychologist John Suler described the 'online disinhibition effect' in 2004: people often say things online that they would hold back from saying face to face.
story:
Declan first saw the comment on Sunday night, on the class chat where everyone shared their science projects. Lily-Anne had posted her poster about nocturnal animals, owls with big yellow eyes, and underneath it someone had written, "This is baby stuff. A kindergartner could do better." The name on the comment was Tommy. That was the part that made no sense. Tommy held doors for people. Tommy said "excuse me" to chairs he bumped into. In person, Tommy was the politest kid in Ms. Smith's class, and Declan had watched him for two days now, waiting for the mean version to appear. It never did. Tommy passed Lily-Anne her glue stick in art without a word about her poster.

Declan felt a twist of guilt, too, because on Sunday he had laughed at the comment before he saw who wrote it. He decided to test something. In the computer lab, he sat where he could see Tommy's screen, and he watched Tommy type a reply to Ms. Smith's homework thread, delete it, type something sharper, and hover over send. The moment Ms. Smith walked past, Tommy minimized the window so fast his shoulders seemed to contract, pulled in tight like he'd been caught.

After school, Declan cornered him at the lockers. "You wrote that thing about Lily-Anne's poster."

Tommy's face went red. "It was just online," he muttered. "It doesn't count the same."

"It counts to her. She's redoing the whole thing."

Tommy stared at his shoes for a long moment. Then he said, "My brother calls it the online disinhibition effect. People say stuff online they'd never say to your face." He shut his locker. "That's me, isn't it."

Declan waited, not letting him off the hook but not yelling either.

"Okay," Tommy said. "Tomorrow. I'll tell her in person." He pulled his backpack over one shoulder and actually held the door open on the way out.

activity: the idea that people interpret the same events and ideas differently
knowledge_domain: the idea that people interpret the same events and ideas differently
fact: The Rubin vase, introduced by Danish psychologist Edgar Rubin in 1915, can be seen as either a vase or two faces, but not both at the same moment.
story:
David arrived at the art room early to help Mr. Grant distribute the supplies for the after-school club: poster paper, markers, and a stack of prints Mr. Grant had brought from the community centre downtown. David wanted first pick of the prints, because the best one would go on the club's wall, and he had decided it should be the picture of the vase.

Simona grabbed it before he could. "This face picture is going on the wall," she said, holding it up. Mikaela leaned in and nodded. "Two faces. Obviously."

"It's a vase," David said. "White vase, black background. Look at the shape." He turned the paper toward them, but Simona turned it right back. "Two faces, nose to nose," she said, tracing the outline with her finger.

They argued until Mr. Grant asked what the noise was about. He looked at the print for a second and said only, "That's the Rubin vase," then went back to sorting markers. David stared at the page. He tried to see it as two faces and failed; then he stared so long at the black part that the faces flipped into view, and the vase vanished. He blinked and it was a vase again. He could not hold both at once, no matter how he tried, and he tested this four more times to be sure.

"It flips," he announced. "But you can't see the vase and the faces at the same time. Not both in one moment." Simona tried it, scowled, then said, "Okay, that's real. But it's still a face picture." Mikaela laughed and asked what it was probably called by people who studied pictures. David said, "Rubin vase. A psychologist named Edgar Rubin made it in 1915. Danish guy, apparently." He had no idea how he knew that; he had read it on the back of the print while they argued, where somebody had penciled it in.

Here was the twist: when he turned the paper over to show them, the pencil note continued in Mr. Grant's handwriting. "Whoever sees the faces first, come ask me about the commerce of ideas. You'll see what I mean."

Simona went. David and Mikaela watched from the doorway as Mr. Grant listened, nodded, then pinned the print to the wall sideways.

"There," he said. "Now nobody sees it first."

activity: to revise a draft by cutting weak adjectives and varying sentence length
knowledge_domain: to revise a draft by cutting weak adjectives and varying sentence length
fact: A single precise verb can often replace a weak verb plus an adverb: 'sprinted' says more than 'ran very quickly'.
story:
Brooke sat at her grandmother's kitchen table with her notebook open to the story she'd been drafting for English, a scene about a relay race at summer camp. The screen door banged behind her, and Payton came in carrying a bag of peach slices, because at Grandma's house you could just walk in like that. "Read me the part where Micah grabs the baton," Payton said, dropping into the chair across the table.

Brooke read it aloud. "Micah ran very quickly down the track. He was really tired but he kept going, and he passed the runner very fast, and the crowd was very loud." The room went quiet in a strange way, and even the ceiling fan seemed embarrassed. Payton chewed a peach slice. "It's a race," she said slowly, "but it sounds like everybody's walking through honey. Why does it feel so slow?"

That was exactly the problem, and Brooke couldn't see the cause of it anywhere in the page. She'd written action, short paragraphs, even an exclamation point. She tried reading it again, this time watching Payton's face instead of the words, and noticed her friend's eyes drifting toward the window. Something invisible was dragging. She counted the words in the first sentence: eleven, and six of them weren't doing any work. "Very quickly," she muttered. "Very loud." A suspicious pattern was forming, and she wanted to know if it held all the way through. She devised a quick test: circle every "very" and every adverb, then try deleting it and putting a stronger verb in its place, and see if the race sped up.

Her grandmother, who was notorious in the family for correcting crossword puzzles in pen, leaned over Brooke's shoulder without asking. Brooke crossed out "ran very quickly" and wrote "sprinted." She crossed out "passed very fast" and wrote "blew past." When she read the new version, Payton sat up straight and actually grabbed the edge of the table at the last line. "He sprinted down the track," Brooke read, "the baton hot in his fist, and he blew past the runner in lane two." One verb had swallowed a weak verb plus its adverb whole, and the sentence was shorter and faster at the same time.

"See, 'sprinted' says more than 'ran very quickly,'" Payton said, pointing at the crossed-out words. "You cut two words and gained speed." Brooke flipped to her second draft, where the descriptive forest scene had "walked slowly" and "said quietly," and got the feeling this same trick might be the foundation for fixing the whole story, not just the race. She sharpened her pencil. Next stop: that scene where the coach speaks. "He said very softly to the nervous runner," she read, and rolled her eyes at her own page. "Watch this," she told Payton, and began to write.

activity: to explain why ancient Egyptians built the pyramids and how the Nile shaped their farming
knowledge_domain: to explain why ancient Egyptians built the pyramids and how the Nile shaped their farming
fact: Egyptian farmers used a shaduf, a long pole with a bucket on one end and a heavy weight on the other, to lift river water up to their fields.
story:
Alyssa lugged her poster board into the library and dropped it on the table with a thud. Her report on ancient Egypt was due Friday, and all she had was a title: "The Pyramids and the Nile." She knew the pyramids were huge and the Nile was long, but when Mr. Papadopoulos had asked her why the Egyptians built the pyramids and how the river shaped their farming, she'd mumbled something about "because they wanted to," which he did not dismiss gently. Gerald slid into the chair across from her. "Still stuck?"

"I need a real answer," Alyssa said. "Not just facts, a why." She pulled a book off the shelf, one with a painting of green fields beside a wide blue river, all of it hemmed in by tan desert. She stared at it. If the river flooded every year, she thought, then the water must be what made that green strip possible. But how did farmers get water onto their fields after the flood went down? Did they carry it?

She flipped pages until she found a picture of a strange pole balanced on a post, with a rope and bucket hanging at one end and a lump of clay at the other. A farmer stood beside it, pulling the rope down and letting the weight rise. The caption read: shaduf. She read it twice, then grabbed a pencil and her ruler to test the idea. She balanced the ruler on her finger, taped an eraser to one end, and hung a paper clip and paper cup at the other. When she pressed the light end down, the eraser end swung up. When she let go, the cup end dipped, almost lifting itself.

"Look," she said, turning the book toward Gerald. "They called it a shaduf. A long pole with a bucket on one end and a heavy weight on the other, to lift river water up to their fields." She copied the sentence onto a card, her handwriting quick and crooked. She wrote her new idea underneath: the Nile gave them water and mud, the water grew the grain, and the grain fed the workers who stacked the pyramid stones. The river, she realized, was not the Egyptians' adversary at all. It was like a partner.

"Careful," Gerald said as she piled six more books beside her poster, reckless with enthusiasm. "It's going to topple."

"Let it," Alyssa said, and kept writing.

activity: going to a first sleepover at a friend's house
knowledge_domain: going to a first sleepover at a friend's house
fact: Snoring happens when relaxed tissues in the throat vibrate as air passes through them during sleep.
story:
Hunter had never been to a sleepover before, so he packed his sleeping bag like it might escape: rolled tight, strapped twice, tucked under his arm all the way to Davin's house. The basement rec room had a couch, a TV, a pool table with one wobbly leg, and a carpet that smelled faintly of popcorn. Damian was already there, spreading his bag near the couch, and Davin claimed the spot by the TV so he could reach the controller without getting up.

They played games until midnight, ate too many chips, and whispered about the school talent show until their eyes gave out. Hunter fell asleep thinking this was the best night he'd ever had.

He woke to a sound like a distant chainsaw. It rumbled, paused, then roared again. Hunter sat up in the dark, heart pounding, until he figured out it was coming from Damian, three feet away, mouth open, throat rattling with every breath.

"It's snoring," Davin whispered from across the room, sounding way too calm. "He does this every time."

"How do you sleep through it?"

"I don't. I move." Davin was already dragging his sleeping bag toward the far side of the room, near the pool table. Hunter grabbed his own bag and followed, but the sound seemed to follow too, bouncing off the basement walls.

Hunter lay there with his ears aching and his mind working. He thought about what he'd read once, that snoring happens when relaxed tissues in the throat vibrate as air passes through them during sleep. Damian was lying flat on his back, chin tipped up, which probably let those tissues sag right into the path of the air. If Hunter could change the way air moved through, maybe the noise would stop.

He found a spare pillow in the closet, crept back over, and eased it under Damian's head, tilting it to the side. The chainsaw sputtered, dropped to a purr, then faded to a soft wheeze. Hunter stood there in his socks, feeling like a genius.

"Did you fix him?" Davin whispered, poking his head up.

"I think I turned the vibration off," Hunter whispered back.

In the morning, Damian woke with the pillow still tucked under his neck and blinked at them. "Why am I sideways?"

Davin glanced at Hunter, and Hunter decided to confess. "You snore like a woodshop class. We relocated. Then I gave you the pillow."

"Whoa." Damian sat up. "That's why my sister always slams her door."

Over cereal, Damian asked Hunter to come again next weekend, and even offered him the corner spot by the TV. "Best seat in the rec room," he said. "For the protagonist of last night's adventure."

Hunter laughed so hard he snorted milk, and Davin raised his juice glass like a toast. "To acute hearing," he said. "And pillows."

activity: falling out with a best friend and making up
knowledge_domain: falling out with a best friend and making up
fact: Psychologists distinguish forgiving, which means letting go of resentment, from reconciling, which means rebuilding the relationship; a person can forgive someone without the friendship returning to exactly how it was.
story:
Amelie had not spoken to Lily for four days, and Lily was conducting an experiment about it. Her hypothesis, written on a sticky note above her desk, read: "If I stop being angry, the friendship will convert back to normal." So far the results were poor. Lily had tried letting go of her resentment on Tuesday, lying on her bed and mentally releasing it like a balloon, but Amelie still sat with Uriah at lunch instead of her, and the silence between them had grown so significant that even the class hamster seemed to notice.

The fight itself had started over something almost too small to explain: Amelie had told Uriah that Lily's volcano project looked like "a melted ice cream cone," and Lily had heard about it. Lily had exploded better than the volcano ever did.

"So you're not angry anymore," her mom said Thursday night, chopping carrots in the kitchen. "But you two still aren't talking?"

"That's the weird part," Lily said, frowning at a carrot. "I forgave her. I really did. So why aren't we best friends again? Is that allowed, to forgive somebody and still not be ready?"

Her mom tilted her head, thinking. "You know, I read once that forgiving and reconciling are actually two different things. Forgiving means letting go of the resentment. Reconciling means rebuilding the relationship. You can do one without the other."

Lily stared at her. "Wait. So my balloon was real, it just didn't fix everything?"

"Sounds like it."

This felt like discovering that her science kit had a drawer she'd never opened. She tested the idea the next morning. In the hallway she caught up to Amelie and said, "I'm not mad anymore. Truly. But I might need some time before we're us again." Amelie's shoulders came down from around her ears. "Okay," she said quietly. "Me too, probably."

They walked to class not side by side, but not opposite either, somewhere in between, like two magnets Ms. Diallo would have called "slowly turning." At lunch Amelie saved her a seat, and Lily took it, and the melted ice cream cone joke was so terrible they both laughed anyway.

activity: the difference between a scientific claim backed by tested evidence and a story about one person's experience
knowledge_domain: the difference between a scientific claim backed by tested evidence and a story about one person's experience
fact: Scientists assign people to groups at random so that differences like age or health are likely to be spread evenly, rather than letting people choose their group.
story:
Nolan had one job for Monday: bring in a claim about the new cold medicine from the pharmacy, plus whatever was behind it. He sat down at the computer after dinner and started typing. His aunt had posted a video that afternoon, telling everyone the medicine had cured her cold in two days, and the whole comment section was calling it proof. Two hundred people had shared it. That seemed like a lot of proof to Nolan, so he clicked over to the study his teacher had linked instead.

The study looked boring next to his aunt's video. There was no face, no story, just a chart. Six hundred people with colds had taken either the new medicine or sugar pills, and the groups had been about even at the end. Nolan scrolled down and found a sentence that stopped him: the people had been assigned to their groups at random, by a computer, so that differences like age or health would likely be spread evenly across both groups. They had not been allowed to pick.

"That's weird," Nolan said out loud. He opened a chat window and typed to Mario, who was also doing the homework. "Why wouldn't the study just let volunteers choose whether to try the new medicine? If I had a cold I'd pick the real stuff."

Mario replied, "Because then all the young healthy people would grab the medicine and the old sick people would get sugar pills?"

Nolan stared at that. He tried to formulate his own test of the idea. He grabbed a coin and his notebook, wrote two columns, and invented twenty fake volunteers, deciding their ages by coin flips. Then he let the first ten volunteers "choose," and the ones he'd made younger all picked the medicine. When he compared the columns, the two groups looked lopsided. He flipped the coin again for a random split, and this time the ages landed about even, like the study said.

The next morning he was still checking his notebook on the bus. Mario leaned over. "So the video?"

"An organism is a whole living thing, and a cold is a virus, which some people argue isn't even fully alive," Nolan said. "So one person's video is one person's cold. The study is six hundred people who couldn't stack the deck." He tapped the notebook. "I asked Ms. Watanabe if my coin experiment was a real test and she said it was feasible for a demo, so I'm going to do it in front of the class with volunteers from each row."

Mario flipped one of the paper coins Nolan had cut out during homeroom. "Heads, you present first."

Nolan caught it midair and set it under the document camera.

activity: the idea that prices rise when many people want something scarce and fall when it is plentiful
knowledge_domain: the idea that prices rise when many people want something scarce and fall when it is plentiful
fact: In the Dutch Republic, prices for rare tulip bulbs soared in the winter of 1636 to 1637 and then collapsed in February 1637, when buyers stopped showing up.
story:
Aria pushed through the Saturday market crowd with ten dollars in her pocket and one goal: a basket of strawberries. Last week they had cost four dollars a basket, but today the berry farmer's table was nearly empty and the sign said eight. "Why did they double?" she asked. The farmer shrugged. "Frost took half my crop. Everybody wants what's left." Aria walked away without buying, her mind snagging on something.

She found Trevor and Nikola at the honey stall, where the beekeeper was practically giving jars away at two dollars each. "Too much rain this year," he told them. "My hives produced double. I can't sell it all." Nikola bought three jars. "So strawberries cost more because there aren't many," Aria said slowly, "and honey costs less because there's too much?" Trevor nodded. "Scarcity and plenty. It's like that tulip thing Ms. Kim mentioned in class." Aria remembered only pieces: something about Holland, a long time ago.

"After school we could look it up," Nikola said, and they did. In the library Aria read the facts out loud, making sure she had them right. In the Dutch Republic, prices for rare tulip bulbs soared in the winter of 1636 to 1637, and then they collapsed in February 1637, when buyers stopped showing up. Trevor sat back. "Same rule. Lots of people wanting something scarce, so the price flies up. Then, in one month, the buyers vanished and the whole thing fell apart." Aria copied the dates into her notebook twice so she wouldn't mangle them.

She decided to test the idea on the trading-card craze sweeping her grade. Cards for a certain dragon were selling in the hallway for five dollars each, because only a few kids had pulled one from a pack. Aria traded hers for three dollars' worth of candy, guessing the price would drop. For two weeks she watched, and when a new shipment flooded the store, dragon cards were suddenly everywhere. Nobody would pay a dollar. "You called it," Trevor said at the next market Saturday, where Aria used her acute bargaining sense to get the strawberry farmer's last basket for six dollars, since berries were coming in plentiful again.

"I almost got that backwards, though," Aria admitted. "First I thought the price went up because the cards got prettier." Nikola laughed and handed her a strawberry. Ms. Kim, buying honey at the next stall, waved them over. "Come tell the class about bulbs and dragons," she said. "Both of them. Especially the part where you got it wrong first."

activity: to shade a sphere with a light source to show highlight, shadow and cast shadow
knowledge_domain: to shade a sphere with a light source to show highlight, shadow and cast shadow
fact: On a shaded sphere, the highlight is the brightest spot, on the side facing the light, and its position shows where the light is coming from.
story:
Jace slid his pencil case off the counter so fast that a fork shot off the kitchen table and rang against the floor like a tiny bell. He was getting the good paper out, the thick kind, because tonight he was going to draw a sphere that actually looked round instead of like a flat gray cookie.

Last week his sphere had been the worst one in art class. He could still picture Sydney holding it up, squinting, and asking, "Is this a circle or a potato chip?" Even Mr. Joshi had paused over it longer than he paused over anyone's, which was its own kind of disaster. So tonight Jace had set a lamp on the kitchen table, plopped an orange down in front of it, and grabbed his pencil like a knight grabbing a sword.

Alessia had come over to watch, which made it feel like an actual event. She leaned in with the eagerness of someone about to see a magic trick. "Okay, where do you start?"

"With the shadow part," Jace said, shading the right side dark. He drew fast, then remembered to slow down, because rushing never made anything better. "But watch this. The side facing the lamp, that's where it stays bright."

"Where exactly?" Alessia picked up his first attempt and turned it toward the light. "Because this one looks flat. Which side was the lamp on?"

Jace stopped. That was the problem. His old drawing was shaded everywhere, evenly, like fog, so the lamp could have been anywhere, or nowhere. He looked at the orange on the table. The lamp sat on the left, and the brightest spot sat on the left side of the orange, a small gleaming patch, brighter than anything else on it. Farther right, the orange dropped into shadow, and behind it, on the right, a dark shape stretched across the table. He grabbed his pencil.

"The brightest spot has to be on the side facing the light," he said, shading a small bright patch on the left of his new sphere and keeping everything else darker. "It's called the highlight. And once it's there, you know where the light's coming from."

"Like a sensor," Alessia said. "You look at the bright spot and it tells you the lamp's position."

"Exactly!" Jace darkened the right side, then added the cast shadow stretching away behind the sphere. His hand seemed to accelerate, pencil flying, because now he could see the whole thing in his head: highlight, shadow, cast shadow, the lamp, the table, all of it connected.

When Sydney texted asking about homework, Jace photographed the finished sphere and sent it before he could lose his nerve. The reply buzzed back in ten seconds: "Okay, lamp on the left. Not a potato chip. Framing this permanently."

Alessia laughed so hard she knocked the orange off the table, and it rolled, gleaming, straight under the lamp.

activity: watching a big game with family and friends
knowledge_domain: watching a big game with family and friends
fact: The crowd 'wave' became known worldwide at the 1986 FIFA World Cup in Mexico, so many English speakers outside North America call it the Mexican wave.
story:
Grandpa's living room was so full that Edouard had to sit on the arm of the couch, which everyone agreed was a violation of the couch's constitution, according to Anton, who liked using big words whether they fit or not. On the big screen, the game was tied, and in the stadium the whole crowd rose section by section, arms lifting like a ripple of water, and then sat back down again. Macey jumped up and did it too, and then Edouard, and then even Anton, wobbling on a cushion.

"Do the wave again!" Edouard shouted at the TV, as if the players could hear him.

The cousin visiting from England, who was squeezed into the corner chair, looked confused. "Why do you keep calling it the wave? It's the Mexican wave."

"It's the wave," said Macey. "That's just what it is."

"It's the Mexican wave," the cousin insisted. "Everybody at home calls it that."

Edouard stopped cheering and thought about this. Same movement of the crowd, two different names. Could a thing have two names depending on where you lived? It seemed almost like a trick, or a riddle. Maybe one of them was wrong, or maybe both were right, and the interesting part would be figuring out why. He decided to run a test, the way Ms. Castillo was always suggesting in science class. "Grandpa," he said, "what do you call it when the whole stadium stands up like that?"

Grandpa adjusted his glasses and leaned closer to the screen, which he claimed he was monitoring for replays, though mostly he monitored for snacks. "The wave," he said. "Always has been, since I was a kid. Conventional name around here."

Edouard turned to the cousin. "And you're sure it's the Mexican wave in England? Everybody says that?"

"Everybody," said the cousin. "It caught on at the 1986 World Cup in Mexico. That's where the whole world saw it. So we named it after Mexico."

That was the piece Edouard had been missing. The wave wasn't just something crowds did; it had a birthday, sort of, and it had happened somewhere specific, and the people watching from other countries had stamped the place right into the name. Americans had already been doing it, so they kept their own word, but the rest of the world had discovered it in Mexico in 1986 and never forgot. Two names, one wave, and now he understood both.

"I want to change my vote," Anton announced. "I previously believed Macey. Now I believe everybody."

"That's not how votes work," said Macey.

On the screen, the crowd rippled again, and Edouard leapt up first, arms high. "Mexican wave!" he yelled, and the cousin laughed, and the whole room rose together, Grandpa last, groaning about his knees and reaching for the pretzels anyway.

activity: to use loops and if-then blocks in Scratch to make a game that keeps score
knowledge_domain: to use loops and if-then blocks in Scratch to make a game that keeps score
fact: An 'if then else' block runs one set of blocks when its condition is true and a different set when it is false.
story:
Maria pulled her elastic hair tie off her wrist and snapped it against the computer lab desk, once, twice, thinking. On the screen, her Scratch cat sat under a sky full of falling stars. Every star the cat caught added one to the score. Every star it missed hit the ground and vanished, and nothing happened at all. That was the problem. The whole class would play her game at the sharing fair on Friday, and right now a player could miss forever and never lose.

"You need a lose screen," said Alex, leaning over from the next computer. "Mr. Somsak's example had one."

"I tried that," Maria said. She showed him the pile of blocks. When the score reached ten, the game said "You win" in big letters. But when she added a second block that said "You lose" whenever the score was less than ten, the words "You lose" flashed on the screen at the very start of the game, before anyone had even played. Alex laughed so hard the kid two rows over turned around, and Maria felt her face go hot. It was almost enough to make her delete the lose screen and pretend the game had never needed one.

Finnegan slid his chair over. "Mine did that too. Mr. Somsak fixed it in like ten seconds and I couldn't follow what he did."

"Then we figure it out ourselves," Maria said. She stared at the blocks. The win message and the lose message were running from the same spot, one after the other, every single second. So the game was always checking, always deciding. Something invisible was choosing which words appeared, and it chose "lose" whenever the score was under ten, which was all the time at the beginning. She needed both messages to come from one decision, not two.

"Wait," she said slowly. "There's a purple one. If then else." She dragged it out and nested the win message inside the first empty slot. She put the lose message in the second slot, the one below. "If the score is ten, it runs the top part. Otherwise it runs the bottom."

"Otherwise?" said Finnegan.

"If the condition is false," Maria said. "The bottom set runs instead. One check, two roads."

She clicked the green flag. Stars fell. She caught three, then let one smash into the ground on purpose, and the score dropped to two. Her heart thumped as the checker ran, that hidden thing she could not see, choosing behind the blocks. The screen stayed quiet. She caught seven more stars, one after another, her fingers tight on the arrow keys, and when the score touched ten the words "You win" burst across the sky.

"Now miss on purpose," Alex whispered.

Maria let every star fall. The screen went dark and printed "You lose" in red letters. Finnegan pumped his fist. "No propaganda from the win screen anymore. It only says the truth."

"Only one thing left," Maria said, snapping her hair tie around the mouse cord for luck. She clicked the green flag again and whispered, "Round two."

activity: performing on stage for the first time in a school concert
knowledge_domain: performing on stage for the first time in a school concert
fact: The standard tuning pitch for the A above middle C is 440 vibrations per second, an international standard known as A440.
story:
Brooklyn had never performed on a stage in her life, and in eight days she was supposed to play her violin in front of the whole school. She practiced in the living room every evening while her dad cooked dinner, and every evening the tuner app on his phone glowed the same stubborn message. The little needle kept drifting left of center, and the number at the top of the screen read 440. "Why 440?" she asked. "Why not 400, or 500, or 5?" Her dad shrugged and went back to chopping onions, so Brooklyn decided to find out herself.

The next day she carried the question to Mr. Clarke, the neighbour who had once played trumpet in a navy band. He let her borrow a thin book from his shelf, and she sat on his front steps with it until she found the page. "The A above middle C vibrates 440 times per second," she read out loud, "and it's an international standard." Mr. Clarke tapped the page. "A440," he said. "That's the one every orchestra tunes to." Brooklyn copied the sentence onto an index card so she could cite the book if anyone asked, because Philip had already teased her once about making things up, and she wanted a legitimate source this time.

Then she ran a test. If 440 was the real pitch of that A, her open A string should match it when she played it into the app. She set the phone on the music stand, drew the bow across the string, and watched. The needle hovered, quivered, and sank flat. She turned the fine tuner a tiny bit, played again, and this time the screen flashed green. It wasn't luck; she slid the peg slightly and the needle fell flat, then brought it back and the green returned. There was a real rule underneath the wobbly needle, and now she could hit it on purpose.

Still, eight days of practicing left only so much room for anything else, and she could feel the erosion of her free time as the weekend disappeared into scales and the concert piece. Philip and Raphael came over twice to listen, and Raphael clapped so enthusiastically after her wobbly high notes that she laughed and tried the passage again. "You dropped your elbow on the jump," Philip said, honest as always. She fixed it. The passage came out clean.

On concert night, backstage under the hot lights, disaster struck. A stagehand's cart clipped her case, and when she checked her strings, the A had slipped flat. There was no time for the app, no phone allowed in the wings. Brooklyn closed her eyes, remembered the green flash and the feel of the fine tuner under her fingers, and adjusted by tiny turns, testing each one with a quiet open string. The pitch she heard in her head matched the one under her bow. She walked out, lifted the violin, and drew the A across the strings, and from the piano behind her Mr. Clarke's old friend played the same note right back.

activity: to add and subtract fractions with unlike denominators by finding a common denominator
knowledge_domain: to add and subtract fractions with unlike denominators by finding a common denominator
fact: Multiplying two denominators together always gives a common denominator, though it is not always the smallest one.
story:
Laurence drummed her pencil on the kitchen table and glared at the worksheet. "One half plus one third," she read aloud. "You two are impossible. You don't even fit in the same pizza."

Jackson sat diagonal from her, dunking a cookie in his milk. "Easy. Just multiply the denominators. Two times three is six, so thirds and halves both become sixths. Three sixths plus two sixths equals five sixths. Boom."

"That's not what the book says to do, though," said Laurence. "It says find the least common denominator."

"Same thing, isn't it?"

She tried it her way first, hunting for the smallest number both denominators would accommodate. For two and three, six was the only choice, so Jackson's shortcut had worked by accident. She scribbled two more problems. One fourth plus one sixth: Jackson's trick gave twenty-fourths, four twenty-fourths plus six twenty-fourths, ten twenty-fourths. But twelve worked too, and twelve was smaller. She wrote it both ways, checked them against each other, and sat back.

"Your way is right," she admitted, "but sometimes it gives you a great big answer you have to wrestle down. Ten twenty-fourths simplifies to five twelfths. That's an extra step. You're doing more work for the same answer, like rowing a boat with no rudder and hoping you drift the right way."

Jackson folded his cookie wrapper into a little boat and steered it across the milk with his pinky. "My boat has a rudder, thank you. And it's fast."

"You have ten minutes before Mom drives us to practice," said Yacine from the counter, where he was supposed to be quizzing them both. He pointed his flashcards at the clock.

Laurence attacked the last three problems, testing Jackson's trick on each one, crossing out when a smaller denominator fit and simplifying the giants when they didn't. Her pencil flew. Jackson folded a second boat.

"If we finish before the clock," he said, "I race you. Kitchen table to front door."

"Deal," said Laurence, and wrote the final answer, five twelfths, underlined twice.

activity: getting a first phone and learning to use it responsibly
knowledge_domain: getting a first phone and learning to use it responsibly
fact: Two-factor authentication asks for a second proof, such as a code sent to your phone, so a stolen password alone is not enough to get into an account.
story:
Alexia's new phone sat on her desk like a small black rectangle of glory. Mr. Sinclair had allowed the class to keep their devices out for the morning's tech lesson, which mostly meant Kody leaning across the aisle to admire his own reflection in the screen. "You've had it for two days," Kaydence whispered from the next desk. "Have you even texted anyone yet?"

"Only my grandma," Alexia admitted. "She sent eleven dog stickers."

Before Kaydence could tease her, the phone buzzed. A message appeared: Your login code is 483021. Do not share it with anyone. Alexia frowned. She hadn't tried to log in to anything. Then it buzzed again with another code, and a third, like a tiny angry drum in her pocket.

"That's weird," she said, turning the screen so Kaydence could see. "I didn't ask for a code. Why would they send me one?"

Kaydence peered at it. "My sister gets those when she signs in to her game. The code only comes when somebody's typing in your password."

Alexia felt the thought condense in her head, all the scattered buzzing suddenly forming one clear idea. If the code was arriving, someone had her password. Someone was trying the door right now, and the only thing standing between them and her account was this string of numbers on her screen. "So somebody knows my password," she said slowly. "But they can't get in without this code."

"That's two-factor authentication," Kaydence said with a shrug. "My mom calls it the second lock."

Mr. Sinclair wandered past their desks, surveying the room with the sparse attention of a man who had learned that middle schoolers left alone with phones would eventually invent their own disaster. He stopped when he saw Alexia's screen. "Codes you didn't ask for, hm? What do you suppose that means?"

"Someone has my password," Alexia said. "But they can't get in, because the code comes to my phone, not theirs. A stolen password alone isn't enough." She felt oddly proud, like she'd solved a puzzle before the teacher handed out the clues.

"Change the password," Mr. Sinclair said, "and don't tell anyone the new one. Not even in dog stickers."

She changed it right there, tapping carefully, then texted her grandma the news. A dog sticker arrived within seconds, this one wearing a tiny party hat.

"Good news travels fast," Kaydence said.

"The best kind of commerce," Alexia said grandly, and Kody, still admiring his reflection, asked if that was a band name.

activity: going on a family trip away from home
knowledge_domain: going on a family trip away from home
fact: Motion sickness happens when the eyes and the balance organs in the inner ear send the brain conflicting signals about whether the body is moving.
story:
The ferry pulled away from the dock while Maeva sat in the enclosed lounge with her new book, determined to finish three chapters before the island appeared. Ten minutes later her stomach rolled, and she had to put the book down and stare at the carpet.

Last summer, in the back seat of the car on the winding road to her grandmother's house, the same thing had happened. She had blamed Francis's driving, then the smell of the oranges, then her own bad luck. This time she started thinking instead. Both times she had been reading. Both times the world around her was moving. Maybe her eyes, glued to a still page, kept telling her brain that nothing was moving, while something else inside her ears, some balance thing, kept insisting that everything was moving. Two messages about the same question, and they could not both be right.

"Want a ginger candy?" Tessa asked, dropping into the seat beside her. "My mom swears by them, but I think that's controversial. Francis says they're magic."

"Everything is controversial with Francis," Maeva said. "Come outside with me. I want to test something."

The negotiation took a moment, since Tessa had just gotten comfortable, but Maeva won by pulling her friend's sleeve. On the open deck, the wind was cold and the windows had fogged so that the water had disappeared behind them. Maeva planted her feet, fixed her eyes on the far horizon where the sea met a grey band of sky, and let the boat's rise and fall become part of what she watched. Slowly, her stomach settled.

"It worked," she reported. "Watching the horizon. My eyes and my ears agreed for once." She thought of all those orange-scented miles to her grandmother's house, and how she could have looked out the window the whole time. She hadn't even tried. She filed that away.

"Three chapters, though," Tessa said, nodding at the book under Maeva's arm.

Maeva held it up against the fogged glass, where her breath was beginning to condense in a small circle. "Maybe I'll read through this little window. Then my eyes will see the sea moving, too."

"Risky," said Tessa.

"I like risky," said Maeva, and opened the book.

activity: cooking or baking a meal for the family
knowledge_domain: cooking or baking a meal for the family
fact: Water should never be poured on a grease fire, because it turns to steam instantly and spreads the burning oil; turning off the heat and covering the pan with a lid smothers it.
story:
Maelie flipped open her notebook, the one she called her cookbook memoir, even though it only had three recipes in it so far. Tonight she was adding a fourth: crispy chicken for her parents and her little brother. She had butter, breadcrumbs, and a bottle of oil that smelled faintly of synthetic lemon, which she decided would irritate nobody once the chicken was golden.

"Brooklynn says frying is easy," Maelie told her mother, who was folding laundry at the table, half watching. "You just get the oil hot and listen for the sizzle."

Her mother nodded and kept sorting socks. Maelie poured the oil into the pan and turned the burner to medium. She arranged the breaded pieces on a plate like little soldiers waiting for orders.

The first batch sizzled exactly the way Brooklynn had promised, and Maelie could hardly stand still. She flipped each piece with tongs, and the kitchen started to smell like a real restaurant. Then she got greedy and slid in four pieces at once. A bit of breading dropped off, and suddenly the pan flared. Orange flames licked up over the oil, and the smoke alarm let out one sharp, angry chirp.

Her mother was beside her in two steps, calm and fast. "Watch." She reached past the faucet, and Maelie expected her to grab a cup of water, but instead her mother turned off the burner and slid the lid straight over the pan, like closing a book. The flames shrank, flickered, and vanished. "Water would have made it worse," her mother said. "It turns to steam instantly and spreads the burning oil everywhere. Lid and no heat, that's it." She lifted the lid a crack, peeked in, and set it back down. "Grease fires are smothered, not drowned."

Maelie stared at the pan. So the fire needed air, and the lid took the air away, and the water would have thrown burning oil all over the stove. She wrote all of it at the top of her memoir page in capitals: NEVER WATER. TURN OFF HEAT. LID ON.

Ten minutes later the second batch came out perfect, and she carried the platter to the table with her chin high. Her little brother grabbed a piece before anyone sat down, and her father laughed and poured the milk.

"Chef Maelie," he announced, raising his glass.

"Dinner is served," she said, "and nothing is on fire."

activity: to fast, pray or keep a day of rest for part of a day as their family does and explain why
knowledge_domain: to fast, pray or keep a day of rest for part of a day as their family does and explain why
fact: Islam excuses people who are sick or travelling from the Ramadan fast, and they make up the missed days later.
story:
Brielle woke up on the sofa bed at her aunt's house with her throat on fire and her forehead hot as a kettle. It was the second day of Ramadan, and she had been awake before dawn yesterday to eat with everyone, and she had fasted the whole day, and now today was ruined.

"I can't miss a fast," she told her cousin Lou, who was stacking plates for the evening meal under the canopy of grapevines in the backyard. "It's only day two. What if I just don't drink anything anyway?"

Lou looked at her like she had suggested swimming in January. "You have a fever. Tia already called your mom."

Brielle pulled her blanket tighter. The problem wasn't today, exactly. The problem was the feeling that the month was a wall you had to climb in one unbroken piece, and she had already fallen off. She thought about it while the ceiling fan ticked around and around. Maybe the rule wasn't a wall. Maybe it was more like the tiles on the ceiling, square by square, and you could move one to another place and the floor still got covered. She sat up too fast and the room tilted, which proved something.

At sunset everyone gathered under the vines, and her uncle set out dates and lentil soup, and Brielle, wrapped in the blanket, said, "I'm going to make it up later. After Ramadan, when I'm better. A whole day, later."

Her mom stopped pouring water. "Who told you that?"

"Nobody. The fever, and the travelling. We took the train here, it took six hours, and yesterday I felt fine so I fasted anyway, but I was thinking, if someone's sick or travelling, it doesn't count against you. You just owe the days."

Her aunt laughed and pointed at her with a spoon. "She figured it out like a detective."

"Grandma says it every year," said Lou. "I thought you knew."

"I didn't," said Brielle, and the relief felt like cold water. She looked at the dates. "So I eat now, and later I pay it back, and it counts the same."

"Eat," said her uncle. "You have a month of fevers to make up for, starting with this soup."

Brielle reached for the bowl and broke her fast on purpose, for the first time ever, and it felt strange and good at once. "I'll recruit you to fast with me on the makeup days," she told Lou. "All three of them. You in?"

Lou groaned, but he was already grinning. "Fine. But you're buying the breakfast."

activity: to follow a recipe to bake muffins from start to finish including preheating the oven
knowledge_domain: to follow a recipe to bake muffins from start to finish including preheating the oven
fact: Double-acting baking powder releases gas twice: once when it gets wet in the batter and again when it is heated in the oven.
story:
Sofia had never baked anything without her mother hovering nearby, so when Kacey's kitchen was finally empty except for the two of them, she set the muffin tin on the counter like it was a treasure. The recipe card belonged to Kacey's grandmother, and the handwriting was so loopy that Sofia had to hold it under the window light to read "double-acting baking powder" in the ingredients list.

"Double-acting," Kacey said, popping the lid off the tin. "That's a weird name."

"Maybe it's like an emperor," Sofia said, thinking of the unit on Rome they'd just finished. "One title isn't enough, so it gets two." Kacey laughed and cracked an egg into the bowl, and a piece of shell slipped in, which Sofia fished out with the edge of a spoon.

The oven had to be preheated first, the card insisted, so Sofia turned the dial and watched the little orange light blink on. Then she measured the flour, the sugar, the powder, stirred in the milk and oil, and noticed something odd as she folded the batter. It seemed slightly puffier than a moment ago, as though it were quietly filling with air.

"Look," she said, tilting the bowl toward Kacey. "It puffed before any heat touched it. So maybe the powder releases gas once when it gets wet, right here in the batter." She paused, chewing her lip. "But then why is it called double-acting? Once isn't double." The oven ticked and hummed behind them, still climbing toward temperature. Sofia, who was usually impulsive about guessing, made herself wait. "If it acts again when it's heated in the oven," she said slowly, "then the batter can sit a few minutes without being ruined. That must be why the recipe doesn't panic about that."

The oven beeped. Sofia slid the tin in, and exactly as she'd predicted, the batter gave a second rise as the heat spread through it, the muffins crowning up golden and fat. "You should advocate for muffins every Saturday," Kacey said, sliding the tray out twenty minutes later and breathing in the warm blueberry smell. Sofia lifted one muffin, broke it open, and watched the steam curl up into the light.

activity: volunteering at a community food bank for the first time
knowledge_domain: volunteering at a community food bank for the first time
fact: In the United States, Feeding America is a nationwide network of more than 200 food banks.
story:
Jacob had signed up for the neighborhood cleanup because his mother said the garage could not hold one more bag of cans, and because Georges had promised there would be doughnuts at the end. Nobody had mentioned that his assigned block was the alley behind the Whitfield Food Bank, where the cleanup was mostly moving boxes of donated soup from a truck to a warehouse shelf.

"The doughnuts better be worth it," Georges said, dropping a box with a thud.

"Careful," said Mohammed, who was already inside arranging cans by label. "If one of those hits your toe, you'll be limping around all summer. No antibiotic required, but still."

It was while Jacob was stacking boxes that he noticed the logo on the truck's side. A bowl with a swoosh, and under it, Feeding America. He had seen that exact swoosh that morning, on a truck parked three streets over. He walked to the loading door and looked out. That truck had different plates, from a city two hours away, and the same logo. So did a van pulling in behind it, with plates from somewhere he couldn't read.

"Hey," he said. "Why do trucks from other cities all have the same logo? Is it stolen?"

"Stolen?" Mohammed came to look.

Jacob had a theory, and theories deserved tests. "Okay, maybe it's one big company that owns all the food banks. Like a chain. Same as hamburger places." He picked up a flyer from the counter by the door, the kind volunteers got on their first day, and turned it over. There it was again, the bowl with the swoosh, and a line about being part of a nationwide network of more than 200 food banks. Not one company with trucks everywhere. Lots of separate food banks, all connected, all over the country, moving food to wherever it was needed. His chain theory had been wrong, which stung slightly, and which he chose not to paraphrase out loud.

Taped inside one of the donated boxes was a folded note in careful handwriting. Mohammed read it aloud: "To whoever gets this soup: I was hungry last winter and this place fed me. Now I have a job. Here is soup for the next person. Signed, a neighbor." Nobody said anything for a second. Georges put the box down very gently, which for Georges was practically a speech.

Ms. Lawson, who ran the warehouse, came over with a clipboard. "You three are my last volunteers for this shift. You coming back?"

Jacob had planned to say no. He had a bike, a summer, a doughnut waiting. But he looked at the trucks in the lot, from three different cities, all part of the same big quiet system, and at the note still in Mohammed's hand, and heard himself say, "Is there a permanent spot open?"

"There is now," said Ms. Lawson, and wrote his name on the clipboard before he could change his mind again. "Thursday, four o'clock. Bring the strong friend."

"That's me," said Georges, flexing one arm and dropping a can with the other.

activity: going on a family trip away from home
knowledge_domain: going on a family trip away from home
fact: Swallowing or yawning opens the Eustachian tubes, which lets air into the middle ear and relieves the pressure people feel in their ears as a plane descends.
story:
Abigail had one objective at Gate 14: get her ears through the flight without the stabbing ache she remembered from last summer. She stood at the window watching the baggage carts, her boarding pass folded into quarters in her pocket, while her little brother, Leo, swung his dinosaur between his knees and hummed.

Across from her, Parker was unwrapping a pack of gum with slow, deliberate care, like it was treasure. "My mom gets three packs every time," Parker said. "Want one? It helps me chew through takeoff and landing." Abigail took a piece but kept turning the problem over. Chewing helped, she knew that much, but she wanted to understand why. She watched an old man two seats down open his mouth wide in a yawn, then press a finger under his ear like he was checking something.

"Notice anything?" Abigail asked Parker, nodding toward the man. Parker squinted. "He yawned right before we started boarding. Like clockwork."

The flight was smooth until the descent, when the captain's voice came over the speakers and the plane tipped its nose down toward the gray blanket of clouds. Abigail's ears began to feel as if someone was pressing on them from the inside. In the row ahead, Leo started to wail, small and miserable, tugging at his ears with both fists.

Their mom dug through the seat pocket, found nothing, then signaled to the flight attendant, who leaned down and handed Leo a small cup of juice. Leo swallowed, hiccupped, swallowed again, and the crying stopped as if someone had turned a dial. Abigail watched the whole thing happen twice more: Leo fussed, Leo drank, Leo was fine.

She tested it herself. She yawned, deliberately, and felt something give way inside her ear with a faint pop, and the pressure eased. She swallowed, and it eased further. "Parker," she whispered, "watch. Yawn, then swallow." Parker did, and his eyes went wide at the pop.

"That has to be the probable answer," Abigail said. "Swallowing or yawning opens the Eustachian tubes, and that lets air into the middle ear and relieves the pressure." Parker rolled the word around. "Eustachian. Sounds like a dinosaur Leo would like."

By the time the wheels touched down, Leo was asleep with the empty juice cup still in his hand, and the little dinosaur was propped against the window, facing the runway.

activity: to describe their family and pets in a new language using full sentences
knowledge_domain: to describe their family and pets in a new language using full sentences
fact: French uses the verb "avoir" (to have) to give age: "J'ai douze ans" means "I am twelve," but word for word says "I have twelve years."
story:
Chase stood at the French booth at the cultural festival, holding a card with his family written out in careful sentences. Ms. Oyelaran from school had told them to practice describing their families to at least three strangers, and the humid air under the tent made the paper go soft in his hands. He had it all ready: "J'ai une sœur. J'ai un chien. J'ai onze ans." Or at least he thought he did.

"Une seconde," said the woman at the booth, squinting at his card. She tapped the last sentence. "You wrote something like 'I have eleven years.' That's not how we say it." Chase stared at the line. "But it says j'ai means I have," he said. "It does," she agreed, smiling.

His friend Gloria appeared beside him with a paper cup of mango juice. "What's wrong?" Chase showed her the card. "In French, age uses avoir, to have. So 'J'ai douze ans' means 'I am twelve,' but word for word it says 'I have twelve years.'" Gloria said it aloud twice, then laughed. "So if I want to say my cat is old, I'd say the cat has a lot of years?" The booth woman nodded, still grinning.

Chase tried an experiment in his head. He took the English sentence apart, almost the way you might decompose a stanza in a poem to see how each line worked, and then put it back together in a new order. "J'ai onze ans," he said slowly. Then, bolder: "Mon chien a deux ans. Il est petit et noir." The woman clapped once and called over another festival volunteer to listen.

"Encore," the volunteer said, which Chase guessed meant again. He had come to the festival thinking he would just recite his card and leave early, but now he wanted to stay until his sentences came out without him checking the paper at all. He borrowed a fresh card, wrote his whole family in French, wrong-word traps and all, and marched toward the Haitian food booth to find victim number two. "Bonjour," he began. "J'ai une mère très impressionnante."

activity: saying goodbye to a grandparent who has died
knowledge_domain: saying goodbye to a grandparent who has died
fact: Japan's Obon festival, held in mid-August in most regions and in July in some, honors the spirits of ancestors, who are believed to return home for a visit.
story:
Lily had exactly one hour before the lanterns were released, and the paper lantern in her hands was still blank. Her whole family had written messages on theirs already. Her aunt had painted a tiny blue heron, her grandmother's favorite bird, on hers. Lily's cousin had drawn a mountain. Only Lily sat with her brush hovering, because she could not decide what to say to Grandma, who had died in the spring.

"You're staring at it like it's a test," her cousin said, crouching beside her on the riverbank. Around them, relatives rearranged picnic blankets and passed around cold tea while the sun dropped lower behind the hills. "There's no wrong answer."

Lily turned her phone over in her lap. Her friend Ty had texted that morning from home, complaining that he had to miss soccer for two more weeks because of his concussion, and that missing the season finale felt inevitable now, since the last game was Saturday no matter what. She had almost envied him, in a strange way. His problem had a date and a rule and a doctor. Hers just sat in her chest like a stone.

Here was what Lily kept turning over: her cousin's family in another part of Japan had already done this. In July, they had gone to the temple and lit lanterns, and Lily's mom had said something confusing about it then. Lily had assumed, back home in the spring, that she had missed her one chance, that the day for honoring Grandma had passed while she was studying for a geography quiz. But now she was here, and everyone was doing it again, tonight, in the middle of August. She looked down the riverbank at the stacks of lanterns waiting for dusk. "Wait," she said slowly. "Obon happens at different times?"

Her cousin nodded. "Mid-August here. July for some places, like where my aunt lives." That was all, but it was enough. Lily felt something loosen. There was no single locked door she had failed to walk through. Grandma was believed to come home for a visit, and the visit had simply not started yet here.

She set her brush to the paper and wrote what she would have said at the kitchen table: that she had learned to make Grandma's cucumber salad, badly the first time and better the second, and that the blue heron lamp in the entryway was still lit every evening. Then, because Grandma had always paused before meals to emphasize that the first bite should be the best one, Lily added one line: "Save the first bite for me."

When the monk struck the bell, the lanterns went onto the water one by one, and Lily eased hers in with both hands. It wobbled, steadied, and drifted out toward the dark center of the river, where it joined a slow constellation of small lights floating home.

activity: to swim twenty-five metres front crawl with side breathing
knowledge_domain: to swim twenty-five metres front crawl with side breathing
fact: In front crawl, the body rolls from side to side with each stroke, and the breath is taken as part of that roll rather than by twisting the neck alone.
story:
Paisley's swim team shared the rec centre with the track club, so on Thursday evenings she crossed the infield of the running track, cut between the hurdles stacked by the fence, and went straight to the pool doors. Her objective for the week was written on the whiteboard in the changeroom: twenty-five metres of front crawl, breathing to the side, no stopping.

She could do the distance easily. The problem was her neck. Every time she needed air she craned her head up and around while lying flat on the water, and by the third length her neck ached so badly she had to switch to breaststroke. On Saturday it hurt to turn her head in class when Quinton called her name.

Vada was in the next lane, resting at the wall. "You look like a chicken," she said. "Your head's doing all the work."

"Chicken," Quinton said from the block above them, because he had heard, and because he never missed a chance.

Paisley thought about that in the water. Her head was doing all the work. She watched the swimmer in lane four, a girl from the older squad who made the crawl look slow and easy. The girl didn't crane anything. Her whole body rolled, first one side, then the other, and the breath came out of that roll like it was part of it, not a separate thing she added on. When she rolled right, her face turned with her shoulder and her mouth cleared the water. Then she rolled back down.

Paisley tried it. She pushed off, pulled with her right arm, and rolled her whole side toward the ceiling instead of twisting her neck. Her mouth found air. She rolled back, pulled with the left, rolled the other way, and breathed again. Her neck didn't hurt. She stopped at the flags, floating, and worked out why the girl had looked slow: rolling side to side made each stroke longer, so fewer strokes covered the same water.

Mr. Harper, guarding in his chair, called the next set. "Two lengths, crawl, whatever breathing side you like."

"Both sides," Paisley said. It came out more assertive than she'd planned, like a claim she was ready to back up.

"Then show me," Mr. Harper said.

She pushed off the wall. Right arm, roll, breathe. Left arm, roll, breathe. At the far wall she flipped around, which wasn't required but felt right, and came home the same way, her body rocking from side to side down the lane. She touched the tiles and looked up.

"That," said Mr. Harper, "was twenty-five metres of front crawl. Side breathing and everything."

Vada slapped the water. "Do it again," she said. "I want to count your strokes."

activity: to mediate an argument between two friends without taking a side
knowledge_domain: to mediate an argument between two friends without taking a side
fact: A "position" is what someone demands, while an "interest" is the reason they want it; people with clashing positions often have interests that could both be met.
story:
Arianna arrived at Lola's birthday party just as the piñata went up, a paper dragon glittering in the sun, and she could already tell something was wrong. Lola and Leila stood under it, arms crossed, both pointing at the same folding chair beside the snack table.

"That's my seat," Lola said. "It's my party."

"I saw it first," Leila said. "I put my juice box on it."

Arianna's dad had told her once that a "position" is what someone demands, while an "interest" is the reason they want it. She hadn't really understood until now, watching two best friends glare at one plastic chair. Maybe, she thought, they each wanted the seat for different reasons. That was an idea she could actually test. She pushed through the crowd of kids, heart pounding like she was about to dismantle the piñata herself.

"Before we fight," she said, "nobody move. I'm going to ask one question each." The kids around them went quiet, which felt enormous, like she was holding the whole party in suspense. "Lola, why that seat?"

"It's the only one in the shade," Lola said. "The sun's giving me a headache."

"Leila, why do you want it?"

"It's next to the speakers. I want to feel the bass when the music starts. I always sit near speakers."

Arianna nearly laughed out loud. They weren't fighting about a chair at all. Lola wanted shade. Leila wanted sound. The chair was just the position each of them was demanding. "Okay," she said, moving fast before anyone could argue again, "Leila, take the chair, but move it right under the big speaker by the fence. Lola, there's a whole strip of shade behind the ice cream table, and there's a cushion on the bench there."

The two girls looked at each other. Then Leila dragged the chair across the grass with a scraping sound, and Lola claimed the shady bench, testing the cushion like a queen testing a throne. Within a minute they were both laughing about the molten chocolate cake batter Lola's mom was carrying out of the kitchen, candles already lit, flames wobbling.

Then came the twist. Lola's mom looked at the empty spot where the folding chair used to be and frowned. "That chair was for the birthday girl," she said. "It had my good luck charm tied to it."

Lola jumped up. "Mom, the charm!" Leila gasped and turned the chair upside down, and there, tangled in the metal crossbar, hung a tiny silver elephant on a red string.

"You found my luck," Lola said, hugging her.

Arianna grinned and cut herself the first slice of cake.

activity: hosting a grandparent who comes to stay for a week
knowledge_domain: hosting a grandparent who comes to stay for a week
fact: The sense of smell naturally declines in old age, a change called presbyosmia.
story:
Grandpa arrived at noon on Saturday, and by Sunday morning Ryan had already burned the toast twice without anyone noticing but himself. The second time, smoke curled up to the ceiling and the kitchen smelled like a campfire, yet Grandpa sat at the table reading his paper, calm as anything. When Ryan waved the smoke away and opened a window, Grandpa glanced up. "Something burning, champ?"

Ryan slid the blackened slice into the trash and tried to figure it out. Grandpa wasn't ignoring the smell, because when Ryan cracked an egg a minute later, Grandpa said, "Mind the butter, don't let it spatter." He could hear fine. He could see the smoke if he looked. Ryan thought about how his own nose governed whether he noticed food going wrong, the way a smoke alarm governed the whole house, and he wondered if Grandpa's alarm had simply gone quiet.

After breakfast, Ryan called his friend Eshaal, whose grandmother lived with her family. "Does your nani ever miss smells?" he asked. "Like toast burning right in front of her?" Eshaal laughed. "All the time! My mom took her to the doctor. It has a name, presbyosmia. The sense of smell naturally declines in old age." Ryan wrote the word on the back of a grocery receipt, feeling the bizarre shape of it in his mouth when he said it aloud.

He decided to test it. Monday morning he set up a little ritual before breakfast: he put the toaster far from the table, stood beside it while it worked, and counted to forty. He kept the window cracked so any smoke would drift toward him and not sit invisible over Grandpa's head. Tuesday he tried bread from the freezer, which cooked slower, and nothing burned at all. "You've been hovering over that toaster like a hen," Grandpa said, smiling over his paper. "New job?"

"Sort of," Ryan said. "Toast duty." He set a golden slice on Grandpa's plate, still warm, and poured the coffee before it could scorch.

activity: bringing home a first pet and learning to care for it
knowledge_domain: bringing home a first pet and learning to care for it
fact: Xylitol, a sweetener in some sugar-free gum and candy, makes a dog's body release insulin and can cause a dangerous drop in blood sugar.
story:
The adoption day at Riverside Park had turned the field near the duck pond into a maze of pens and banners, and Abigail walked through it with her mother, trying to look calm while her heart hammered. She had been saving allowance since October, and she had done the reading, the whole stack of library books about feeding schedules and crate training and hygiene, twice. The puppy she chose was a scruffy brown mutt with one ear that stood up and one that flopped, and the shelter volunteer handed over the leash and said, "Her name's Pickle, but you can change it." Abigail kept it.

Jackson and Matthieu biked over as soon as she texted a photo, and the four of them, counting Pickle, settled under a big oak while Abigail's mother went to buy lemonade. Pickle wobbled around on the grass, chewed a stick, sneezed, then wandered over to the backpacks piled against the tree. Before anyone could move, she had her whole head inside the side pocket of Jackson's bag, and she came out chewing something silver.

"Gum," Jackson said, going pale. "I had almost a whole pack of sugar-free stuff in there."
