Abigail counted the wrappers on the grass. Three pieces gone, maybe four, and Pickle was small, maybe ten pounds. Then she turned the empty pack over and read the ingredients out loud, and stopped at one word she half remembered from a poster at the vet's office. "It says xylitol." She looked up. "That's the one. Xylitol makes a dog's body release insulin, and it can cause a dangerous drop in blood sugar."

Matthieu was already on his phone finding an animal clinic two streets away. "Can dogs even get low blood sugar?" he asked as they ran, taking turns carrying Pickle because she was too little to keep up.

"That's the bad part," Abigail said. "You can't see it happening. She might act fine right now and still be in trouble, so they have to check."

The clinic smelled like disinfectant and dog, and the vet tech took Pickle straight back the moment Abigail explained about the gum. In the waiting room, Jackson sat with his hood pulled over his face, and Abigail's mother arrived breathless from the park. "It's my fault," Jackson kept saying, until Abigail sat down next to him and said, "It's my dog. And nobody knew. Now we know."

The vet came out after twenty minutes that felt like an hour and said they had caught it in time; Pickle would stay on fluids and they would watch her sugar, but she would be fine. Abigail asked if she could go in, and the tech said visiting was voluntary, they didn't usually allow it, but for a new owner they'd make an exception.

Pickle was drowsy on a towel, her crooked ears flat, and she thumped her tail once when Abigail knelt down. Jackson appeared in the doorway holding the gum pack, which he had flattened completely. "This is going in the trash at home," he said, "and I'm buying you a lock for your backpack too."

"You're buying her one," Abigail said, and scratched Pickle behind the ear that stood up.

activity: building a project for the school science fair
knowledge_domain: building a project for the school science fair
fact: The independent variable is the one thing a scientist changes on purpose, and the dependent variable is what gets measured to see the effect.
story:
Elliot spread six paper airplanes across the kitchen table like evidence at a trial. The science fair was in two days, and his poster board sat blank on the counter, which made his stomach drop every time he looked at it. He had planes with pointed noses, planes with wide wings, planes folded from magazine pages, and one lopsided thing he refused to call symmetrical no matter how he squinted at it. His best flights had gone nine feet, eleven feet, and somewhere under the couch.

Taryn arrived carrying her own half-finished poster and dropped into the chair across from him. "I need your opinion because my mom won't give a verdict, she just says everything is wonderful." She pulled out her notebook. "But first, what is happening here? Which one of these is the experiment?"

"That's the problem," Elliot said. "I tested everything at once. Different wings, different paper, different throws. Ms. Ngo circled a note on my draft that says, 'What is your independent variable?' and I don't know what that means, so I just sort of stopped."

Taryn tapped the notebook against her chin. "We learned that in September. The independent variable is the one thing you change on purpose. The dependent variable is what you measure to see the effect." She pointed at his planes. "So when you threw some harder than others, you were changing stuff by accident. That's why your numbers are junk."

Elliot sat up straight. "So if I only change the wing shape, and keep the paper and the throw the same, then the distance I measure shows what the wings did." He pushed all the planes aside except three, folding new ones from the same notebook paper, identical folds except for the wings: one narrow, one medium, one wide.

He marked a line on the kitchen floor with painter's tape and told Taryn she was excluded from throwing duty, since her tosses always came out softer. "You're the measurer. Same person throws every time, same person measures every time."

"Fine, but you owe me help with my poster tonight," she said, flipping open the tape measure.

He threw each plane five times, careful and level, the way he'd practiced. Taryn called out the distances and he wrote them down. The wide wings won three rounds out of five, and the numbers finally made a pattern he could actually see, even though the cause, the air doing whatever it did, stayed invisible.

"Eleven feet," Taryn announced on the last throw. "That's your winner, and my mom was right, everything is wonderful."

Elliot grabbed the marker and wrote his question at the top of the poster board: How does wing shape affect flight distance? Then, underneath, he wrote the words he'd been missing. "Independent variable: wing shape. Dependent variable: distance." He underlined both and said, "Taryn, you're staying for dinner, I owe you a title page."

activity: to read contour lines on a topographic map to find the steepest slope of a hill
knowledge_domain: to read contour lines on a topographic map to find the steepest slope of a hill
fact: The U.S. Geological Survey's standard 7.5-minute topographic maps use a scale of 1:24,000, so one inch on the map equals 2,000 feet on the ground.
story:
Matthew spread the map across the kitchen table and weighted its curling corners with a butter dish and two mugs. The map had come from his grandfather's closet, brown and crisp like a giant leaf, covered in squiggly brown lines. Somewhere on it was Hickory Hill, and somewhere on Hickory Hill was the steepest slope, and if Matthew could find it before dinner, he and Rylie and Talon would have a plan for Saturday that did not involve wandering around the woods getting temporary hope every time the ground tilted upward.

"The trick is the lines," Talon had told him at school. "Where they squish together, the hill is steep. Where they spread out, it's flat." Fine, except the lines squished in three different places on Hickory Hill, and Rylie wanted the steepest one, measured, because Rylie did not accept "probably" as an answer. She was bringing a stopwatch and intended to invest the whole afternoon in timing their climb.

Matthew laid his ruler between the contour lines at each squished spot. The lines at the western slope were packed so tight they nearly touched, like the stripes on a candy wrapper. On the east side they had breathing room. He measured the patch of packed lines end to end: an inch and a half, edge to edge.

Then he hunted for the scale. In the bottom corner, in tiny print, the map announced itself as a U.S. Geological Survey 7.5-minute topographic quadrangle, scale 1:24,000. Below it, in plainer words: one inch on the map equals 2,000 feet on the ground. He checked it twice. One inch, two thousand feet. So his steep patch was three thousand feet across, and the ground rose several contour intervals within it, which meant climbing the west face would feel like stairs, while the east face was an illusion of difficulty, a long gentle ramp that only looked intimidating from the road.

The phone buzzed. Rylie, of course.

"West side," Matthew said. "Three thousand feet of nearly straight up. Bring the stopwatch and maybe a rope."

"Bring a rope," Rylie repeated, and he could hear her grinning. "For a hill."

"My grandpa's map doesn't lie," Matthew said, and he folded the old paper carefully along its worn creases and set it on top of his backpack by the door.

activity: to add and subtract fractions with unlike denominators by finding a common denominator
knowledge_domain: to add and subtract fractions with unlike denominators by finding a common denominator
fact: The least common denominator is the smallest number both denominators divide into evenly; for quarters and sixths it is 12.
story:
Mya slid her worksheet across the table and tapped the problem she had been stuck on for ten minutes: one quarter plus one sixth. She had written one over twenty-four and six over twenty-four, then crossed both out and started over with one over forty-eight.

"Why do you keep picking giant numbers?" Auston asked, leaning over. He was the fastest kid in math club, which normally embarrassed Mya, since she was supposed to be the fastest too.

"Because twenty-four is a nice round number, and I know it works," she said. "Four goes into it, and so does six."

Malcom, on her other side, was stacking his pencil on top of his eraser like a little tower. "Round doesn't matter here. Try smaller."

"There's no smaller one," Mya said. "Twelve? That's too easy. It's an illusion that a small number could work for both."

Malcom knocked over his tower. "Look. The least common denominator is the smallest number both denominators divide into evenly." He wrote 12 on her paper. "For quarters and sixths, it's twelve."

Mya stared at it. Four went into twelve three times, and six went into twelve twice. She did the problem twice, once with twelve and once with her twenty-four, and got one half both ways.

"They give the same answer," she said slowly. "But the twelve one has smaller numbers."

"Now you get it," Auston said.

Mr. Morin walked past their table and paused. "One over twenty-four plus six over twenty-four? That's your answer down there, Mya, but it wasn't the shortest road."

"I changed my mind about twenty-four," Mya said. She flipped her paper over and wrote a new problem for Malcom: one sixth plus one quarter, in that order. "Your turn. And no stacking pencils."

Malcom picked up his pencil and wrote 12 at the top of the fraction.

activity: getting a first phone and learning to use it responsibly
knowledge_domain: getting a first phone and learning to use it responsibly
fact: The phone Martin Cooper used for the first handheld cell phone call weighed about 1.1 kilograms (2.5 pounds).
story:
The phone was gone. Charlie had set it on the corner of her desk exactly where Mr. Lewandowski had said phones could sit during the science unit, and now that corner held only a dust smudge. She checked her pocket twice, then her backpack, though she already knew the answer, because she remembered watching the screen dim toward black while she labeled her polymer samples. Plastic, she had written, is a polymer, and she'd looked up just long enough to see the phone sitting there. It had been there at 10:15. It was not there at 10:40.

"Adley," she whispered, "call my number."

Adley pulled her own phone out of her sock, because nobody put phones in backpacks anymore, and dialed. Across the room Emile stiffened. Charlie watched him the way you watch a suspect in a movie, and when a faint buzzing started, it did not come from Emile's direction. It came from the supply counter, from inside the tray of sponges they used for spill cleanup. The sound was muffled, almost nothing, and the porous sponges were doing their work, swallowing the ring the same way they swallowed water.

"Some phones in 1973 would've knocked that tray off the counter," Mr. Lewandowski said, wandering past with his coffee. "Martin Cooper made the first handheld cell phone call on a phone that weighed 1.1 kilograms. That's 2.5 pounds." He kept walking.

Charlie lifted the top sponge. Nothing. The second. Nothing. Her heart was going fast now, and her hands felt too big for the job. Under the third sponge, wrapped in a paper towel, sat her phone, its case still vibrating against the counter. Someone had hidden it, and whoever it was had wanted the sponges to hinder anyone hearing it ring.

She carried the tray back to her desk, set the phone down, and looked around the room slowly. Adley mouthed, who? Emile's face had gone pink, and he was very busy copying a diagram he had already copied.

"You dropped it near the counter," Emile said, not looking up. "I was keeping it safe."

"From what?"

He sharpened his pencil for a long time. Then he said, so quietly she almost missed it, "You got a phone before me."

activity: falling out with a best friend and making up
knowledge_domain: falling out with a best friend and making up
fact: The 'fundamental attribution error', named by psychologist Lee Ross in 1977, is the habit of blaming someone's behavior on their character while overlooking the situation they were in.
story:
Asher saved the back seat of the bus for Peter, the way he had every morning since second grade, and Peter walked right past it. He dropped into the seat across the aisle next to Addilyn and stared out the window like the parking lot was the most interesting thing in the world.

"Fine," Asher muttered. Three weeks ago Peter had skipped Asher's birthday sleepover with one text: can't come, sorry. No reason. No "happy birthday." Asher had spent three weeks deciding what that meant about Peter, and the answer was simple: Peter was selfish. He'd rather stay home playing games than sit in Asher's basement eating pizza at midnight. Defiant, even, the way he'd ignored every message since.

But something nagged at him. Peter had been excited about the sleepover. He'd talked about it for days, argued about who got the air mattress, promised to bring his dad's old projector. That didn't fit. Peter wasn't acting like a selfish person. He was acting like a person with something heavy going on, and Asher couldn't see what. He decided to test it. If the problem was Peter's character, Peter would be rude to everyone. If the problem was something in Peter's life, there would be a crack somewhere.

He leaned over the seat. "Addilyn, did Peter talk to you in science yesterday?"

"A little." She lowered her voice, eager to be the one with news. "He asked if the pharmacy on Miller Street is open on Sundays. I said yes, and he asked if they fill prescriptions fast. Weird question, right?"

Weird unless somebody needed medicine. Asher turned around, and there it was: Peter's backpack, half open, and inside it a folded hospital visitor pass with the name GRANDMA WU printed on it. Asher's whole theory collapsed in two seconds.

"You could have just told me," Asher said.

Peter's shoulders went stiff. "I didn't want the whole bus knowing my grandma had a stroke. She's still in there. I go every Sunday, that's why I missed the sleepover. I wasn't being a jerk."

"I know. I figured it out." Asher gripped the seat back. "My mom calls it the fundamental attribution error. This guy Lee Ross named it in 1977. It's when you blame somebody's behavior on their character and overlook the situation they were in. I did it to you for three whole weeks."

Peter finally looked at him. "Three weeks?"

"Every day. It was terrible." Asher moved across the aisle, and Peter shoved his backpack over to make room. "So, redo? Sleepover this Friday, air mattress, projector, everything?"

"Only if you verify with your mom first," Peter said, and for the first time in weeks he grinned. "And I get the air mattress. Deal?"

"Deal," Asher said, and shook on it as the bus pulled out of the lot.

activity: competing in a spelling bee
knowledge_domain: competing in a spelling bee
fact: Noah Webster's 1828 'American Dictionary of the English Language' promoted simpler spellings such as 'color' instead of 'colour', which became standard in the United States.
story:
The spelling bee had moved to the public library this year, and Brooke sat in the third row of folding chairs between shelves of atlases. Round four, and the scores were cumulative now, so every letter counted twice as much as before. She listened as Claira spelled "harbor" without the u, and Claira's shoulders seemed to contract with relief when the judge nodded.

Then it was Brooke's turn. "Your word is colour," said the judge.

"Colour," Claira whispered from her chair, loud enough for half the room to hear. "My cousin in Canada spells it that way. It's not wrong there."

The judge raised a hand for quiet. "In this bee, we follow American spellings. But the contestant may ask for the word in a sentence."

Brooke stood very still. If colour was a real spelling somewhere, then the American version had to come from somewhere too, some moment when the two paths split. She needed the split. "Sentence, please," she said.

"The colour of the sky changed before the storm."

She spelled it c-o-l-o-r, and the judge rang the small bell that meant correct. But afterward, while the others lined up for snacks, she pulled Claira toward the reference desk, where Mr. Berg was reshelving a heavy volume.

"Where would the American spelling have started?" she asked him. "Not the word itself. The spelling."

He smiled and led them to a locked case, unlocked it, and let them lean close to a thick old book. "Noah Webster's 1828 American Dictionary of the English Language," he said. "It promoted simpler spellings, such as color instead of colour, and those became standard in the United States."

Claira traced the page with one finger. "So my cousin is spelling it the old way," she said, "and I'm spelling it Noah Webster's way."

Brooke copied the title onto her hand in small letters. "Round five," she said, "I'm ready."

activity: to learn a traditional dance or song well enough to perform it at a community gathering
knowledge_domain: to learn a traditional dance or song well enough to perform it at a community gathering
fact: In the Philippine dance tinikling, two people tap bamboo poles on the ground twice and then clap them together on the third beat while dancers step in and out.
story:
Hazel stood at the edge of the community hall floor, watching two pairs of bamboo poles click and clack like giant mouths. Mr. Cohen had announced that the tinikling group would perform at the spring gathering in three weeks, and Rihanna had already signed up. Hazel wanted to be up there too, but every time she stepped toward the poles, her feet turned to stone.

She tried again during the first practice. Tap, tap, clap. The dancers slid their feet in and out between the poles, and Hazel jumped too late. The bamboo snapped shut on her ankle, and she hobbled to the wall to sit down. It stung, but what bothered her more was the mystery of it. The good dancers weren't faster than her. Some of them were grandparents. So what were they hearing that she wasn't?

She watched Rihanna's turn next, and it struck her that the poles and the feet weren't two separate things fighting each other. The pole tappers hit the ground twice, then clapped the poles together on the third beat, and the dancers stepped in on the ground beats and pulled out before the clap. Was the answer to stop counting the poles and start counting three beats, over and over? Maybe she could test it by counting out loud.

Back on the floor, she murmured, "One, two, clap. One, two, clap." Her ankles stayed clear. When she lost the count, a pole nipped her heel; when she found it again, she was through to the other side. "You sound like a bird," Rihanna laughed, and Hazel laughed too, still counting.

"Those bamboo poles are counterfeit," a woman from the dance group said, holding one up. "Real ones are heavier." She tapped out the rhythm beside Hazel so they could practice together.

By the end of the evening, Hazel danced the full pattern twice without a single snap, and Mr. Cohen wrote her name on the performance list. Many families who had migrated from the Philippines had brought the dance here, he said, and taught it to their descendants and to neighbours like her.

"One, two, clap," Hazel whispered, and stepped in.

activity: to give a two-minute speech with an opening hook, three points and a closing
knowledge_domain: to give a two-minute speech with an opening hook, three points and a closing
fact: Glossophobia is the name for fear of public speaking, and it is one of the most commonly reported fears.
story:
Victoria stood at the free-throw line, which was painted perpendicular to the sideline, and pretended the gym was full of people instead of empty bleachers. On Monday it would be full. Every seventh grader had to give a two-minute speech with an opening hook, three points, and a closing, and Ms. Adeyemi had booked the gym so they could practice on the actual stage.

Her cue cards were a mess. She tried to compress forty facts about honeybees into three points, but the words crawled together on the card like ants. Worse, her hands had started shaking, and she was only talking to the bleachers.

Spencer was pacing near the door, mumbling his hook about vending machines. "Your hands are shaking," he said, pointing.

"So are yours," Victoria said. His fingers trembled around his own cards, and he hid them behind his back, which was terrible camouflage because she had already seen.

"That's not a thing, right?" Spencer said. "Like, not a lot of people get it?"

Victoria didn't know. But she had an idea for finding out. Instead of guessing, she could test it. She walked over to Alex, who was practicing by the climbing rope, and asked casually, "If you had to give your speech right now, would your hands shake?"

"Obviously," Alex said. "They're shaking now, and the audience is one basketball."

Victoria counted. She asked nine classmates the same question, one by one, like a scientist collecting samples. Eight said yes, and the ninth, a boy who claimed he felt nothing, held up his water bottle so it rattled against the rope hook. Then Ms. Adeyemi came over, and Victoria asked her too.

Ms. Adeyemi laughed. "There's a word for it, you know. Glossophobia, the fear of public speaking. It's one of the most commonly reported fears."

"Wait," Victoria said. "One of the most common? Like, more than spiders?"

"Reported fears, yes. Look around."

Victoria did. Spencer was shaking. Alex was shaking. The confident boy was rattling his bottle. A pattern, hiding in plain sight, and she had found it by asking. If almost everybody's hands shook, then shaking hands couldn't mean she was about to fail. It just meant she was normal. That changed something. She wasn't fighting her own body anymore; she was just sharing a gym with eight other shaking people.

She grabbed her cards and crossed to the mark on the floor. "Hook," she whispered. "Three points. Close." She raised her voice until it bounced off the far wall. "Have you ever eaten something that came out of a bee's stomach? Because that's what honey is."

Spencer stopped pacing. Alex turned around. Ms. Adeyemi folded her arms and smiled.

Victoria kept going, hands trembling, voice steady, all the way to the closing line.

activity: getting a first phone and learning to use it responsibly
knowledge_domain: getting a first phone and learning to use it responsibly
fact: Phone batteries are lithium-ion, and as they chemically age they hold less charge, so battery life slowly gets shorter.
story:
The phone arrived on a Saturday morning in a cereal box, which Zack thought was a joke until he dug through the cornflakes and found his dad's old phone inside, screen smudged but working. "It's yours now," his dad said. "Rules are on the fridge." Zack read them twice: no phone at the dinner table, no phone after eight, and answer Mom's messages. He slid the phone into a synthetic case that smelled faintly of new sneakers and felt ten feet tall.

By Tuesday he had a problem. On Monday the phone died right after lunch. On Tuesday it died during lunch, halfway through a message from his mom asking him to walk home with Luc. He plugged it in every night until the battery icon was full, and it still quit by lunchtime, every single day, like clockwork running fast.

He began to test ideas. First he guessed it was the games, so on Wednesday he played nothing and only texted Luc. It still died. Then he guessed the messages themselves, so on Thursday he barely used it at all. Dead by lunch again. Whatever was eating the battery, it wasn't anything he was doing. That was strange, because the phone had lasted all day back when his dad carried it. Something had changed inside, something he couldn't see.

He was puzzling over it on the front steps when Mr. Kapoor came by with his watering can, a dented green vessel he'd been using since Zack was in kindergarten. "New phone?" Mr. Kapoor asked, and Zack explained the mystery. Mr. Kapoor nodded slowly. "Lithium-ion," he said. "Chemically ages. Holds less charge as it gets older." Zack stared at the phone in his hand. It wasn't broken and he hadn't broken it. The battery had just grown old and tired, like a sponge that could hold less and less water, and no amount of careful charging would trick it back to new.

The twist came at dinner. Zack laid out his evidence, day by day, and his dad went quiet, then laughed in an embarrassed sort of way. "That's why I gave it away," he admitted. "It kept dying on me too. I figured a new owner would fix it somehow." They took the phone to a repair shop on Saturday, where a technician swapped in a fresh battery while Luc and Zack waited, and Luc begged Zack to hurry, because the school trivia team was starting a group chat that afternoon and Luc, who never missed anything, wanted them both to participate.

Outside the shop, Zack powered the phone on and watched the battery icon climb, green and full. Luc leaned over his shoulder. "First message of the season," Luc said. "Ready?" Zack typed, "Send it."

activity: to put a bandage on a cut and know when a wound needs a doctor
knowledge_domain: to put a bandage on a cut and know when a wound needs a doctor
fact: A cut should be rinsed under clean running water to wash out dirt before it is covered.
story:
The laundromat on Miller Street had a reputation for eating socks, but Matteo still came every Saturday because his mother's shift ended at six and the wash had to be done by then. He had just fed the quarters into the machine when Chace leaned against the rumbling dryer and Yousuf tried to pry a stuck detergent scoop out of its plastic tub. The scoop snapped free, its cracked edge catching Yousuf's palm, and a line of red opened across his hand.

"It's fine," Yousuf said, already reaching for his backpack. "I'll just stick a bandage on it."

"Wait," Matteo said, grabbing the first aid kit his mother kept in the front pocket, because she said laundromats and skinned knees went together. He remembered his own scraped elbow from the skate park last month, when Chace had dragged him to the water fountain before doing anything else. "You have to rinse it first. A cut should be rinsed under clean running water to wash out dirt before it is covered."

"That's what they did at the fountain," Chace agreed. "Your elbow was full of gravel."

Yousuf frowned at the sink in the corner, its tap dripping into a stain the shape of Florida. "That water's gross. I'm not using it."

Matteo tested the tap anyway, running it hard, watching the stream run clear after a few seconds. "It's from the same pipes as the drinking fountain," he said. "If it comes out clean, it's clean running water." He held Yousuf's hand under the flow while Chace dug out the antiseptic wipes and the bandages, one by one, like a magician pulling scarves.

Yousuf hissed at the cold but kept his hand there. Under the water, Matteo could see the cut better, and he made himself look at it properly instead of turning away. The edges were close together, not gaping, and the bleeding was already slowing to a slow ooze. A thin line, sealed edges, that was a bandage job. His mother had shown him a deep gash once, on her own thumb, edges pulled apart and blood that would not stop, and said that kind needed a doctor. This was not that kind. He dried the skin around the cut with a clean paper towel, pressed the bandage across it, and smoothed the ends down.

"See?" Yousuf said, flexing his fingers. "I told you it was fine."

"You were going to bandage it dirty," Chace said. "You'd have sealed the dirt right in there."

"I was not." Yousuf paused, then folded the leftover bandages back into the kit. "Okay, maybe I was. Thanks, Matteo."

The washer buzzed with two minutes left on the cycle, and Matteo realized he had lost count of the dryers. Mr. Kamau, who ran the place and had once threatened to boycott the detergent company over the scoop design, came over with a broom and swept up the broken plastic without being asked. He glanced at Yousuf's bandaged palm, then at the wet sink.

"Good rinse," he said. "The coffee machine's working, if the hero wants a hot chocolate."

Matteo pulled Yousuf's wet, soapy towels from the washer and shoved them into the dryer just as the timer hit zero. "Two hot chocolates," he said. "Yousuf's buying."
